cues.text: Let us turn now to additional innovation methodologies and commercialisation.
Innovation management is usually understood as a sequence of four connected activities.
The first is ideation, where an organisation generates ideas.
The second is selection, where those ideas are evaluated for fit and feasibility.
Fit asks whether the idea suits the organisation's strategy, customers and capabilities.
Feasibility asks whether it can realistically be built and delivered.
The third is implementation, where the idea is developed and tested.
The fourth is commercialisation, where the organisation launches the product or service, reaches customers, captures value and scales.
Notice the point the source stresses about that last stage.
Commercialisation is more than completing a prototype.
A working prototype only shows that something can be made.
To commercialise, you must validate pricing, so you know what customers will pay.
You must validate adoption, so you know whether people will actually use it.
You must validate operations, distribution and support, so you know the service can be delivered, reach customers and be maintained.
And you must validate the economics, so you know the whole arrangement makes financial sense.
Now let us look at five methods, presented in a table with three columns: Method, Purpose, and Applied example.
I will walk through each row in order.
Row one is brainstorming.
Its purpose is to generate diverse ideas before critical evaluation.
The key discipline is sequencing: you collect ideas first and judge them later.
The applied example is exploring ways to remove onboarding friction, that is, the awkward steps that make new users give up when they first sign up for a service.
Row two is SWOT.
Its purpose is to diagnose internal and external position.
SWOT looks at strengths and weaknesses inside the organisation, and opportunities and threats in its environment.
The applied example is evaluating whether a fintech can enter a new region.
Row three is Blue Ocean Strategy.
Its purpose is to create uncontested market space through value innovation, and to look beyond current customers.
Instead of fighting rivals for the same buyers, you open a space where competition is not the main issue.
The applied example is offering an affordable, simplified service for previously underserved users.
Row four is TRIZ, pronounced "treez".
Its purpose is systematic inventive problem-solving using recurring contradiction patterns.
The applied example is improving equipment protection without making maintenance inaccessible.
Notice the tension: more protection tends to make the equipment harder to reach for servicing.
Row five is Jobs to Be Done, abbreviated JTBD.
Its purpose is to understand the progress customers seek in a particular context, rather than only product features.
The applied example is a farmer who needs to know when to sell produce, not merely own a dashboard.
The farmer's real need is the decision, not the screen.
Let us now deepen three of these methods.
Blue Ocean value innovation seeks differentiation and cost advantages together, by changing the basis of competition.
A practical tool here is the eliminate-reduce-raise-create grid.
It asks four questions about accepted industry features.
Which should disappear entirely?
Which should shrink?
Which should be improved?
And which new features should be introduced?
Be careful about two misunderstandings.
Blue Ocean is not synonymous with abandoning all competitors, and it is not the same as offering the lowest price.
TRIZ originated in systematic engineering invention.
Its central idea is the contradiction, which occurs when improving one characteristic worsens another.
A common reaction is to accept the trade-off immediately and settle for a compromise.
TRIZ asks you instead to seek a design principle that resolves the contradiction.
Return to our example: protect the equipment, yet keep maintenance accessible.
The aim is a design that achieves both.
Jobs to Be Done focuses on three kinds of job: functional, emotional and social.
A functional job is a practical task to accomplish.
An emotional job concerns how the customer wants to feel.
A social job concerns how the customer wants to be seen by others.
The source also adds an important caution: validate the proposed job through customer research.
A job you have imagined is a hypothesis, not a fact.
Next, three organisational examples.
Apple's design-thinking example highlights integrating human needs and usable product design.
Toyota's lean approach illustrates continuous improvement, removal of waste, quality at source, and respect for people.
Procter & Gamble's open-innovation example illustrates external collaboration for ideas and capabilities.
Remember the qualification the source gives.
These are frameworks applied to organisations.
They are not proof that a single method caused every business outcome.
Success in real firms has many contributing causes.
Now to governance.

Organisations should create innovation governance, which includes resource allocation, transparent selection, experiment owners, decision criteria, risk limits, intellectual property agreements, customer validation and commercial launch support.

In plain terms: decide who gets resources, choose openly, name someone responsible for each experiment, set the criteria for decisions, limit the risk you will take, settle who owns the intellectual property, test with real customers, and support the launch.
Governance should encourage diverse ideas and learning while maintaining evidence-based decisions.
Outcomes to measure include adoption, incremental margin, customer benefits and strategic fit.
Incremental margin means the additional margin the innovation earns.
Finally, the worked framework selection.
Imagine a proposed new agricultural service where user needs are unclear and revenue is uncertain.
The sequence is as follows.
Begin with design research, to understand the users.
Then use a lean MVP, a minimum viable product, to test a willingness-to-pay assumption, meaning whether farmers will actually pay.
Use agile iterations for delivery, building and improving in short cycles.
Partner with local cooperatives through open innovation, bringing in outside knowledge and reach.
And require stage-gates, which are formal checkpoints, before committing substantial investment.
The lesson of this example is that the methods solve different uncertainties.

Design research addresses unclear needs, the lean MVP addresses uncertain revenue, agile addresses delivery, open innovation addresses capabilities and access, and stage-gates control investment risk.
Choosing a method means first asking which uncertainty you face.
